name: THE SUN'LL COME OUT TO-MARROW BURGER (comes with bone marrow)

recipe.history:
Bone marrow — the fatty, gelatinous tissue that fills the hollow cavities of large bones — is one of the most ancient foods in human history. Archaeological evidence from Homo erectus sites dating back nearly a million years shows that early humans cracked open animal bones with stone tools specifically to access the marrow inside, suggesting that the pursuit of this rich, calorie-dense fat was a central organizing activity of early human behavior. In Europe, roasted marrow bones were a standard feature of aristocratic dining from the medieval period through the Victorian era; the Victorians ate it with small spoons from standing bones at formal dinners, scooping out the trembling, butter-soft fat and spreading it on toast. In Southeast Asia and the Middle East, bone marrow has never gone out of fashion — Vietnamese pho achieves its depth partly from long-simmered marrow bones, and in various Iraqi and Iranian preparations roasted marrow is still considered a celebratory luxury. The flavor of roasted bone marrow is often described as the most concentrated beef experience possible: rich, unctuous, slightly sweet, and so deeply savory it borders on transcendent.

Bone marrow's reemergence in fine Western dining is largely credited to British chef Fergus Henderson, whose 1999 cookbook "Nose to Tail Eating" and his London restaurant St. John placed roasted bone marrow with parsley salad at the center of a movement to reclaim forgotten, "ugly" cuts and preparations. Henderson's roasted marrow bones inspired a generation of chefs to revisit the marrow in all its forms, and by the mid-2000s it was appearing on tasting menus and gastropub boards across the English-speaking world. Its journey onto the burger was championed most visibly by chef Daniel Boulud, whose DB Burger at DB Bistro Moderne in New York City featured a short rib and foie gras filling inside the patty, accompanied by bone marrow — a burger that redefined what the format could be. From fine dining it filtered down into the broader burger culture, where roasted marrow spread over the top of a patty or stirred into compound butter became a marker of serious intent.

I first roasted bone marrow at home on a winter night when I was trying to impress someone I was slightly too nervous to cook for, which meant I had chosen something I had never made before — a strategy I do not recommend but have employed more than once. I set the femur halves cut-side up on a foil-lined pan, slid them into a very hot oven, and watched through the oven door as the marrow began to bubble and separate from the bone, the fat rendering from white to translucent in real time. When I pulled them out and spooned the quivering, steaming fat onto thick slices of toast scattered with parsley and capers, the smell alone was enough to end any lingering anxiety in the room. The person across the table went quiet in the way that people go quiet when they are eating something that requires full attention. That silence, I have come to understand, is the best review bone marrow can receive.

The philosophical case for cooking a burger patty to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — becomes almost self-evident when bone marrow is involved. Marrow is pure rendered fat, the most concentrated expression of beefy richness that exists. Spooned over a patty and allowed to melt down through the cheese and crust, it creates a burger of almost reckless luxury. But that luxury requires a foundation: a patty that is still juicy, still pink, still alive with its own fat and moisture. An overcooked patty, dry and grey at its center, would simply be drowned by the marrow, becoming a vehicle for fat rather than a partner to it. At medium rare the beef's own fat is fully rendered and present, the juices are retained, and the marrow adds its layer on top of something already magnificent. Medium rare is the only temperature that gives bone marrow a worthy partner.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend, preferably with some brisket), freshly ground
4 center-cut beef femur bones, halved lengthwise by your butcher (about 3 inches each)
1/2 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
2 tbsp capers, drained and roughly chopped
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C). Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack. Keep oven at 450°F for the marrow.

6. Roast the bone marrow: Place bone halves cut-side up on a foil-lined baking sheet. Season marrow with flaky salt and pepper. Roast at 450°F for 15 to 20 minutes until the marrow is bubbling, has pulled away from the bone slightly, and is just beginning to melt. Remove from oven and set aside. When cool enough to handle, scoop out marrow from the bones using a small spoon or narrow spatula. Keep warm.
7. Make the parsley-caper gremolata: Combine finely chopped parsley, capers, minced shallot, lemon juice, lemon zest, and olive oil. Season with flaky salt. Toss to combine. Set aside.
8. Make the horseradish cream: Whisk together sour cream, prepared horseradish, Dijon mustard, and lemon juice. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

9. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder immediately before cooking.
10. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
11. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Top each patty with a slice of gruyère immediately.
12. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting loosely with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
13. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
14. Assemble: Spread horseradish cream on both cut faces of each bun.
15. Place arugula on the bottom bun and red onion slices. Set the medium-rare gruyère-topped patty on top.

16. Spoon a generous tablespoon of roasted bone marrow over the top of the patty, letting it melt down over the cheese. Scatter a spoonful of parsley-caper gremolata over the marrow. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt.
17. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately before the marrow cools.
